title: Prophets of the exile and the return

intro.text: These pages cover the prophets of the exile and the return: Daniel and Ezekiel among the captives in Babylonia; Haggai and Zechariah, who urged the rebuilding of the house of the LORD in the second year of Darius; Malachi; and the two prophets named in Nehemiah's account of the plots against him, Shemaiah and the prophetess Noadiah.

Ezekiel dates his words by the years of Jehoiachin's captivity, Daniel by the years of the kings of Babylon, of Darius the Mede and of Cyrus, and Haggai and Zechariah by the years of “Darius the king”, whom Ezra calls “Darius king of Persia”. Malachi gives no date.

The date and authorship of Daniel, the authorship of Zechariah 9–14 and whether “Malachi” is a name are disputed. Each page shows the views with their holders, traditional and critical side by side, and gives the readings of the visions as views, never as verdicts.

prophets.name: Daniel
prophets.title: “Daniel the prophet” in the words of Jesus (Matthew 24:15)
prophets.tagline: A captive of Judah at the court of Babylon, from Nebuchadnezzar to Cyrus.

claim.text: The book opens in “the third year of the reign of Jehoiakim king of Judah”, when Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem and “the Lord gave Jehoiakim king of Judah into his hand”. Jehoiakim and Daniel do not meet in the text.

Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar the dream of the great image and its meaning, and the king made him “ruler over the whole province of Babylon”. Later he interpreted the king's dream of the tree and counselled him to “break off thy sins by righteousness”.

quote.text: Thou art this head of gold.

claim.text: At Belshazzar's feast Daniel read the writing on the wall, reminded the king how Nebuchadnezzar had been humbled, and was proclaimed “the third ruler in the kingdom”. That night Belshazzar was slain. Daniel dates two visions by Belshazzar's first and third years.

quote.text: TEKEL; Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.

claim.text: Darius set Daniel first of three presidents and “thought to set him over the whole realm”. Bound by his own decree, he had Daniel cast to the lions, and at dawn found him unhurt. Daniel dates his prayer and the word of the seventy weeks by Darius's first year.

quote.text: My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions’ mouths, that they have not hurt me

claim.text: “Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus”, and “prospered … in the reign of Cyrus the Persian”. His last vision is dated “in the third year of Cyrus king of Persia”. No words between Daniel and Cyrus are recorded.

quote.text: Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams.

claim.text: Daniel's book tells no call. It says that God gave the four young men of Judah “knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom”, and Daniel understanding of visions and dreams, before they stood before the king.

how.text: “The secret” of the king's dream was “revealed unto Daniel in a night vision”, after he and his companions asked mercy of “the God of heaven”; Daniel then blessed God for it.
He interpreted what others saw: the king's dream of the image, the king's dream of the tree, and the writing on the wall.
Later he had dreams and visions of his own, and wrote them down: “he wrote the dream, and told the sum of the matters.”
Gabriel is named twice as the one who makes him understand. In the last vision “a certain man clothed in linen” appears, and “one like the similitude of the sons of men” touches his lips.
In Darius's first year he “understood by books” the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolation that the word of the LORD gave to Jeremiah, and prayed “with fasting, and sackcloth, and ashes”.
Before his last vision he mourned three full weeks, eating “no pleasant bread”.
The book never says that the word of the LORD came to Daniel, and it never calls Daniel a prophet; it uses “prophet” only of Jeremiah and of “thy servants the prophets”.
Jesus speaks of “the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet” (Matthew 24:15; the King James text of Mark 13:14 has the same words).
At Daniel 2:4 the Chaldeans answer the king “in Syriack”.
Driver (1891) notes that the book is written “partly in Hebrew, partly in Aramaic”, the Aramaic running from the words “O king” in 2:4 to the end of chapter 7.

message.theme: The Most High rules the kingdoms of men

claim.text: Daniel blesses God who “removeth kings, and setteth up kings”; the watchers' decree, the voice from heaven and Daniel's word to Belshazzar all say that the Most High gives the kingdom “to whomsoever he will”.

quotes.text: the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will

message.theme: A kingdom that shall never be destroyed

claim.text: The stone cut out without hands becomes a mountain that fills the earth; to one like the Son of man is given an everlasting dominion; and the kingdom is given to “the saints of the most High”.

quotes.text: the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed

claim.text: Daniel would not defile himself with the king's meat; his three companions would not bow to the golden image; Daniel kept praying three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem.

quotes.text: But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods

claim.text: Daniel's prayer confesses the sins of “our kings, … our princes, and … our fathers”, and asks the Lord to hear for his own sake and for the city called by his name.

quotes.text: we do not present our supplications before thee for our righteousnesses, but for thy great mercies

claim.text: The last vision ends with Michael standing up, “a time of trouble, such as never was”, the deliverance of those written in the book, and the awaking of “many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth”.

quotes.text: many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt

quote.text: Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days; and let them give us pulse to eat, and water to drink.

words.to: Arioch, captain of the king's guard

quote.text: Destroy not the wise men of Babylon: bring me in before the king, and I will shew unto the king the interpretation.
There is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets, and maketh known to the king Nebuchadnezzar what shall be in the latter days.
break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor
the God in whose hand thy breath is, and whose are all thy ways, hast thou not glorified
O king, live for ever. My God hath sent his angel, and hath shut the lions’ mouths

signs.label: The king's dream of the great image

claim.text: Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar the dream itself: an image with a head of gold, breast and arms of silver, belly and thighs of brass, legs of iron and feet of iron and clay, broken by a stone “cut out without hands” that became a great mountain. He told its meaning: the king is the head of gold; after him come another kingdom, a third of brass and a fourth strong as iron and divided; and the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed. The text names only the first kingdom.

signs.label: The king's dream of the tree

claim.text: A great tree reaching to heaven is hewn down at the word of “a watcher and an holy one”, its stump left in the earth “till seven times pass over him”. Daniel told the king: “It is thou, O king”.

At Belshazzar's feast the fingers of a man's hand wrote on the plaister of the wall. Daniel read it: “MENE, MENE, TEKEL, UPHARSIN”, and gave its meaning, ending “Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.”
Cast into the den under the decree of Darius, Daniel was found at dawn unhurt: “no manner of hurt was found upon him, because he believed in his God.”

In Belshazzar's first year Daniel saw four great beasts come up from the sea: like a lion with eagle's wings, like a bear, like a leopard with four heads, and a fourth “dreadful and terrible” with iron teeth and ten horns, among which a little horn spoke great things. “The thrones were cast down, and the Ancient of days did sit”, and “one like the Son of man” came with the clouds of heaven and was given an everlasting kingdom. One who stood by told him the beasts are four kings, the fourth “the fourth kingdom upon earth”, and the horns ten kings, after whom another shall rise and “wear out the saints of the most High” for “a time and times and the dividing of time”.

signs.label: The ram and the he goat

claim.text: In Belshazzar's third year Daniel saw in vision, at Shushan by the river Ulai, a two-horned ram pushing west, north and south, broken by a he goat from the west with a notable horn; four horns rose in its place, and from one a little horn that took away the daily sacrifice. He heard “Unto two thousand and three hundred days; then shall the sanctuary be cleansed.” Gabriel explained: the ram is “the kings of Media and Persia”, the goat “the king of Grecia”, its great horn “the first king”, four kingdoms “shall stand up out of the nation”, and “in the latter time of their kingdom” a “king of fierce countenance” shall stand up and “be broken without hand”.

While Daniel prayed, Gabriel came “about the time of the evening oblation” and told him: “Seventy weeks are determined upon thy people and upon thy holy city”; from the going forth of the commandment to restore Jerusalem “unto the Messiah the Prince” shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks; after the sixty-two weeks “shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself”; and in the midst of the last week “he shall cause the sacrifice and the oblation to cease”.

signs.label: The last vision by the Hiddekel

claim.text: In the third year of Cyrus, by the great river Hiddekel, Daniel saw a man clothed in linen and was told “what shall befall thy people in the latter days”: three more kings in Persia and a fourth richer than all, a mighty king whose kingdom is divided toward the four winds, long wars of the kings of the south and of the north, a “vile person”, in whose days “the abomination that maketh desolate” is placed, a king who magnifies himself above every god, and then Michael standing up, a time of trouble and the resurrection. He was told to shut up the words “till the time of the end”, and heard of 1,290 and 1,335 days.

word.text: Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar that he would be driven from men and eat grass as oxen, “and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men”.

reported.text: Twelve months later, as the king boasted of “great Babylon, that I have built”, a voice came from heaven, and “the same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar”. At the end of the days his understanding returned and he praised the Most High.

word.text: Daniel read the last word of the writing: “PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians.”

reported.text: The chapter goes on: “In that night was Belshazzar the king of the Chaldeans slain. And Darius the Median took the kingdom”.

claim.text: Twelve chapters. Six tell of Daniel and his three companions at the courts of Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar and Darius the Mede (1–6). Four visions follow, dated by the years of Belshazzar, Darius and Cyrus (7–12). The stories speak of Daniel in the third person; the visions are mostly told by Daniel himself.

scripture.text: Daniel 1 closes with “And Daniel continued even unto the first year of king Cyrus.” His last dated vision is “in the third year of Cyrus king of Persia”.
The last words to him are a promise: “go thou thy way till the end be: for thou shalt rest, and stand in thy lot at the end of the days.”

tradition.text: Josephus writes that Daniel “built a tower at Ecbatana, in Media”, that the kings of Media, Persia and Parthia were buried in it “to this day”, and that its keeper was a Jewish priest. He adds that Daniel, “now he is dead”, is remembered by the books he left, but does not say where he died.

Benjamin of Tudela, who travelled between 1165 and 1173, describes “the sepulchre of Daniel” at Shushan, and tells how its coffin was moved from one bank of the river to the other until the Persian ruler Sinjar had it set in a coffin of crystal and hung from the middle of the bridge.

questions.question: When was the book of Daniel written, and by whom? (Views in the order of their holders' dates.)

views.label: By Daniel, in the sixth century BC
views.holders: E. B. Pusey (1864); C. F. Keil (1872); R. Dick Wilson in ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Keil holds that the testimony of synagogue and church to the book's “composition by the prophet Daniel, rests on a solid foundation”, and that in antiquity only the Neo-Platonist Porphyry doubted it. Pusey calls the book “either Divine or an imposture”, and lists among his proofs that the “Testimony of our Lord stands alone, as infallible”. Wilson answers the arguments from the Greek names of instruments and the Persian words, holding that a sixth-century writer “may have known and used borrowed Greek terms”.

views.label: In its present form, in the time of Antiochus Epiphanes, on a basis of tradition
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver argues from the book's place among the Writings rather than the Prophets, the silence of Ben Sira, the Persian and Greek words, and the theology, that it was “not written earlier than c. 300 B.C.”, and that grounds exist which, “though not adequate to demonstrate”, yet “make the opinion a probable one, that the Book, as we have it, is a work of the age of Antiochus Epiphanes”. He adds: “Daniel, it cannot be doubted, was a historical person”.

views.label: The stories (1–6) from the third century BC, the visions (7–12) from 168–165 BC
views.holders: J. A. Montgomery (1927)

argument.text: Montgomery assigns chapters 1–6 to Babylonia, “roughly … to the 3d cent.”, as a collection of stories “based on Jewish and Bab. traditions”, and holds that chapters 7–12 “belong to the first years of the Macc. uprising, 168-165 B.C.”

questions.question: Which are the four kingdoms of Daniel 2 and 7? Daniel names only the first (Babylon, “Thou art this head of gold”); Daniel 8 names Media and Persia and Grecia for the ram and the goat.

views.label: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome
views.holders: E. B. Pusey (1864); C. F. Keil (1872); R. Dick Wilson in ISBE (1915)

argument.text: Pusey's second lecture treats “the four empires, Babylonian, Medo-Persian, Greek, Roman, and the establishment of the kingdom of Christ during the fourth Empire”. Keil speaks of “the Babylonian, the Macedonia, and the Roman world-monarchies” with the Medo-Persian between. Wilson adds that the main dispute is whether the fourth is the Seleucid or the Roman empire, “the former view being held commonly by those who hold to the composition of [Daniel] in the 2nd century BC, and the latter by those who hold to the traditional view”.

views.label: Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece
views.holders: Writers listed by S. R. Driver (1891), among them Eichhorn, Bleek, Westcott, Delitzsch and Kuenen; J. A. Montgomery (1927)

argument.text: Driver notes that the book itself distinguishes the Medes and the Persians and puts “Darius the Mede” before Cyrus the Persian, and says that if the fourth beast of chapter 7 is Alexander's empire, this reading “will be the correct one”. Montgomery takes the fourth beast as Greece by analogy with chapter 8, so that the second kingdom “can be nothing else than Media”.

views.label: Babylon, Medo-Persia, Alexander, his successors
views.holders: Bertholdt, Zöckler and Herzfeld, as listed by S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver records this reading and calls it “less probably” right.

questions.question: Who is the “king of fierce countenance” of Daniel 8:23?

views.label: Antiochus IV Epiphanes, king of Syria
views.holders: Josephus (about AD 93); C. F. Keil (1872); S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Josephus, retelling the vision, says “our nation suffered these things under Antiochus Epiphanes, according to Daniel's vision”. Keil writes that “the little horn denotes Antiochus Epiphanes”. Driver says the description “leaves no question that it is Antiochus Epiphanes, which, indeed, is not here disputed”. No other identification is set out in the sources used for this page.

questions.question: What do the seventy weeks of Daniel 9:24–27 count? (Views in the order of their earliest named holder.)

views.label: A word about Rome and the desolation of Jerusalem
views.holders: Josephus (about AD 93); the Jewish reading after him, as J. A. Montgomery (1927) describes it

argument.text: Josephus writes that Daniel “also wrote concerning the Roman government, and that our country should be made desolate by them”. Montgomery counts “the application to the destruction of Jerusalem” as Josephus's reading and, since him, “the regnant Jewish interpretation”.

views.label: Years counted to the coming and death of Christ
views.holders: E. B. Pusey (1864); the older Christian reading described by J. A. Montgomery (1927)

argument.text: Pusey counts the sixty-nine weeks (483 years) from Ezra's commission in the seventh year of Artaxerxes, 458 BC, to AD 26, which, reckoning the Nativity four years before our era as was commonly believed, he takes to coincide with John's baptism and Christ's anointing; the Messiah “cut off” is Christ. Montgomery describes this line as “the ultimate Christian exegesis”, which found in the passage “chronologically verifiable predictions of the advent of Christ”.

views.label: The persecution under Antiochus Epiphanes
views.holders: J. A. Montgomery (1927); Bleek and Meinhold, as reported by S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Montgomery identifies the anointed one cut off with “the high priest Onias III, who was foully murdered” about 171 BC, and the half-week with the profanation of the temple, 168–165 BC. Driver sets this reading beside the one that ends with Christ, finds difficulties in both, and writes that “it must be left to the reader to decide for himself”.

views.label: Symbolic periods reaching to the end of the world
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872), following Kliefoth

argument.text: Keil reads the weeks as stages of the kingdom of God: “first from the end of the Exile to the coming of the Messias; then from the appearance of Christ to the time far in the future”, and finally the time of “the Antichrist” and his destruction at the last judgment.

questions.question: Does Daniel 11:36–45 still speak of the king of verses 21–35?

views.label: No: from verse 36 it speaks of the Antichrist
views.holders: The interpretation given by Jerome, as reported by C. F. Keil (1872); E. B. Pusey (1864)

argument.text: Keil reports that the church interpretation given by Jerome takes 11:21–35 of Antiochus Epiphanes “and Daniel 11:36-45 of Antichrist”. Pusey contrasts Antiochus's character “with that of the Anti-Christ in Daniel ch. xi.”

views.label: Yes: the same king, Antiochus Epiphanes, to the end of the chapter
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver holds that “in a continuous description, with no apparent change of subject”, it can hardly be right “to refer part to the type and part to the antitype”, though he grants that verses 40–45 “occasion difficulty”.

views.label: The whole vision looks to the end-time
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872)

argument.text: Keil rejects a sudden passing to the Antichrist at verse 36, because by 10:14 the whole revelation concerns “the Messianic future”: what is said of the kings of the north and south “has its aim to the end-time”.

questions.question: Is the Daniel whom Ezekiel names beside Noah and Job (Ezekiel 14:14, 20; 28:3) this Daniel?

views.label: Yes: a younger contemporary, already known for righteousness and wisdom
views.holders: E. B. Pusey (1864); C. F. Keil (1876)

argument.text: Pusey holds that God set beside two great patriarchs “a living saint”, singling out “the great living example of righteous life”. Keil answers that naming Daniel before Job does not warrant “some other older Daniel”, because “the enumeration is not intended to be chronological”.

views.label: Uncertain, or an ancient figure of tradition
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891); J. A. Montgomery (1927)

argument.text: Driver calls it “uncertain”, since “the terms in which Ezek. speaks … seem to suggest a patriarch of antiquity”. Montgomery holds that these passages “cannot refer to the youthful hero of our book, but to a figure of antique and cosmopolitan tradition”.

notSaid: Daniel's book does not name his father, his tribe or his age; it says only that he was among “the children of Judah” chosen from the captives (Dan 1:3–6).
Daniel is not mentioned in the story of the golden image and the furnace (Dan 3); the book does not say where he was.
The book never calls Daniel a prophet; the title is Jesus' (Matt 24:15).
Daniel does not name the second, third or fourth kingdoms of chapters 2 and 7; only chapter 8 names Media and Persia and Grecia.
Who Darius the Mede was is not explained in Daniel; the views are on his ruler page.
Scripture does not say where or when Daniel died.

prophets.name: Ezekiel
prophets.title: “Ezekiel the priest, the son of Buzi” (Ezekiel 1:3), made “a watchman unto the house of Israel”
prophets.tagline: Among the captives by the river Chebar, from the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity.

claim.text: Ezekiel dates his first vision by “the fifth year of king Jehoiachin’s captivity”, and later words by the years of “our captivity”. In the riddle of the eagles he says the king of Babylon “hath taken the king thereof” and led him to Babylon.

Ezekiel never names Zedekiah. He speaks of “the prince in Jerusalem” who would go out through the wall and be brought to Babylon, “yet shall he not see it, though he shall die there”; of a king who broke his oath to the king of Babylon; and of the “profane wicked prince of Israel” whose crown would be taken off.

Ezekiel pictures the king of Babylon at the parting of the way, using divination, choosing Jerusalem. He names “Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon” as the one the LORD would bring against Tyrus, and to whom he would give Egypt as wages for his army.

person.name: Pharaoh king of Egypt
person.note: Ezekiel does not name him; the site's person data links these verses to Hophra (Jeremiah 44:30), and Driver (1891) also names him Pharaoh Hophra.

claim.text: Ezekiel set his face against “Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers”, and took up a lamentation for him.

quote.text: Behold, I am against thee, Pharaoh king of Egypt, the great dragon that lieth in the midst of his rivers

call.label: Visions of God by the river Chebar

quote.text: the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God

claim.text: In the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity Ezekiel saw a whirlwind and fire out of the north, four living creatures with wheels beside them, and above them a throne with a likeness “as the appearance of a man”. “This was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD. And when I saw it, I fell upon my face”.

quote.text: Son of man, I send thee to the children of Israel, to a rebellious nation

claim.text: The spirit set him on his feet and he was sent to Israel, “whether they will hear, or whether they will forbear”, so that they “shall know that there hath been a prophet among them”.

quote.text: Then did I eat it; and it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness.

claim.text: A hand held out a roll “written within and without”, full of “lamentations, and mourning, and woe”; he was told to eat it and go speak to the house of Israel.

quote.text: Son of man, I have made thee a watchman unto the house of Israel

claim.text: After sitting “astonished” among the captives at Tel-abib for seven days, he was made a watchman: if he did not warn the wicked, their blood would be required at his hand; if he warned them, he had delivered his soul.

how.text: “The word of the LORD came expressly unto Ezekiel the priest … and the hand of the LORD was there upon him.” The hand of the LORD comes upon him again before the visions of the temple, the dry bones and the new temple.
The spirit lifted him up and carried him: to the captives at Tel-abib, “in the visions of God to Jerusalem”, and back “into Chaldea, to them of the captivity”.
God calls him “son of man” throughout the book: the words “son of man” stand in 94 verses of the King James text of Ezekiel.

He was told to shut himself in his house and that his tongue would cleave to the roof of his mouth, except when God opened it to speak; his mouth was opened the evening before the fugitive from Jerusalem came.

He was told to “put forth a riddle, and speak a parable”, and to take up lamentations for the princes of Israel, for Tyrus and for Pharaoh; he complained, “they say of me, Doth he not speak parables?”
The elders sat before him in his house to enquire; the people came to hear “as a very lovely song”, but “they hear thy words, but they do them not.”
Thirteen passages are dated by the years of Jehoiachin's captivity, most of them to the month and day.
Driver (1891) dates the call to 592 BC and the latest date in the book (29:17) to 570 BC; Keil (1876) reckons the same two dates as 595 and 572 BC.

message.theme: The glory leaves the temple, and returns

claim.text: In the vision of the sixth year the glory of the LORD departed from the threshold of the house and stood over the cherubims at the door of the east gate; then it “went up from the midst of the city” to the mountain on its east side. In the vision of the new temple it comes back by the east gate and fills the house.

quotes.text: the glory of the LORD came into the house by the way of the gate whose prospect is toward the east

claim.text: Jerusalem, set “in the midst of the nations”, has done worse than the nations round about; the bloody city will be judged and the LORD will not go back.

quotes.text: I the LORD have spoken it: it shall come to pass, and I will do it; I will not go back

claim.text: Against the proverb of the sour grapes, the son does not bear the father's iniquity; the wicked who turns may live, “for I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth”.

quotes.text: Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

message.theme: They shall know that I am the LORD

claim.text: Judgment and restoration alike end with the words “ye shall know”, or “they shall know”, “that I am the LORD”: the phrase “know that I am the LORD” (or “the Lord GOD”) stands in 63 verses of the King James text.

message.theme: A new heart and a new spirit

claim.text: God will give his people one heart and a new spirit, take away the stony heart, and put his spirit within them.

quotes.text: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you

claim.text: Against the shepherds who fed themselves, God will seek his sheep himself and set over them “one shepherd … even my servant David”; Judah and Joseph will be one stick in his hand and one nation, with his sanctuary among them for evermore.

quotes.text: I will seek that which was lost, and bring again that which was driven away

quote.text: Are ye come to enquire of me? As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I will not be enquired of by you.
And thou, profane wicked prince of Israel, whose day is come, when iniquity shall have an end
Son of man, set thy face against the Ammonites, and prophesy against them
Because that Edom hath dealt against the house of Judah by taking vengeance
Behold, I am against thee, O Tyrus, and will cause many nations to come up against thee
Because thine heart is lifted up, and thou hast said, I am a God
Behold, I am against thee, O Zidon; and I will be glorified in the midst of thee

claim.text: “Gog, the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal”.

signs.label: The siege drawn on a tile

claim.text: He was told to portray Jerusalem on a tile, lay siege to it with a fort, a mount and battering rams, and set an iron pan as a wall between himself and the city: “This shall be a sign to the house of Israel.”
He was to lie on his left side 390 days for the iniquity of the house of Israel and on his right side 40 days for Judah, “each day for a year”, bound with bands so he could not turn.

He was to make one bread of wheat, barley, beans, lentiles, millet and fitches, eat it by weight, twenty shekels a day, drink water by measure, and bake it with man's dung “in their sight”: “Even thus shall the children of Israel eat their defiled bread among the Gentiles”. When he protested that his soul had never been polluted, he was given “cow’s dung for man’s dung”. The LORD would break the staff of bread in Jerusalem, where they would eat bread by weight and drink water by measure.

He was to shave head and beard, weigh the hair in balances and divide it: a third burned in the midst of the city, a third smitten about with a knife, a third scattered in the wind; a few bound in his skirts, and of these some cast into the fire.

signs.label: Smiting the hands, stamping the foot

claim.text: “Smite with thine hand, and stamp with thy foot, and say, Alas”; later, “smite thine hands together”.

He brought out his “stuff for removing” by day, dug through the wall at evening and bore it on his shoulder in the twilight; he had been told to cover his face. “And I did so as I was commanded.” “I am your sign: like as I have done, so shall it be done unto them”.
He was to eat his bread with quaking and drink his water with trembling, for the people of Jerusalem would do so.
He was to sigh “with the breaking of thy loins” before their eyes, and when asked why, answer “For the tidings; because it cometh”.
He was to mark two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon, one to Rabbath of the Ammonites and one to Jerusalem, where the king “stood at the parting of the way … to use divination”.

On the day the king of Babylon set himself against Jerusalem, Ezekiel was told to write the day's name and utter a parable of a pot set on the fire, whose scum would not go out: “Woe to the bloody city”.

“The desire of thine eyes” was taken with a stroke, and he was not to mourn. “So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded.” “Thus Ezekiel is unto you a sign”.
On the day the fugitive came, “thy mouth be opened to him which is escaped, and thou shalt speak, and be no more dumb: and thou shalt be a sign unto them”.
He wrote “For Judah” on one stick and “For Joseph, the stick of Ephraim” on another and joined them in his hand before their eyes: “they shall be no more two nations”.

In the sixth year, as the elders sat before him, he was taken by a lock of his head “in the visions of God to Jerusalem” and shown idolatry in the temple courts; men marked on their foreheads were spared; the glory left the house; and at the east gate Pelatiah son of Benaiah died as he prophesied.

Set down in a valley full of very dry bones, he was asked “can these bones live?” He prophesied, and the bones came together, flesh came on them, and breath came in, “an exceeding great army”. “These bones are the whole house of Israel”: God would open their graves and bring them into their own land.

signs.label: The new temple and the river

claim.text: In the twenty-fifth year he was set on “a very high mountain” in the land of Israel, and a man with a measuring reed showed him a temple, its courts and gates, the glory returning, the ordinances of priests and prince, waters flowing from under the threshold to heal the sea, and the land divided among the tribes. The city's name: “The LORD is there.”

word.text: He was told that the desire of his eyes would be taken “with a stroke” and that he must not mourn.

reported.text: “So I spake unto the people in the morning: and at even my wife died; and I did in the morning as I was commanded.”

word.text: He was told that in the day of Jerusalem's fall “he that escapeth” would come to him, and “in that day shall thy mouth be opened … and be no more dumb”.

reported.text: In the twelfth year of the captivity “one that had escaped out of Jerusalem came unto me, saying, The city is smitten”; the evening before, the LORD had opened his mouth, “and I was no more dumb”.

word.text: In the vision he was told to prophesy against twenty-five men at the east gate who gave “wicked counsel in this city”.

reported.text: “And it came to pass, when I prophesied, that Pelatiah the son of Benaiah died.”

word.text: In the eleventh year he said the LORD would bring “Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon” against Tyrus.

reported.text: In a word dated the twenty-seventh year he says that Nebuchadrezzar “caused his army to serve a great service against Tyrus”, “yet had he no wages, nor his army, for Tyrus”, and that Egypt would be given him instead.

claim.text: Forty-eight chapters, with thirteen words dated by the years of the captivity: the call and the signs and visions against Jerusalem (1–24), words against seven nations, Ammon, Moab, Edom, the Philistines, Tyrus, Zidon and Egypt (25–32), and the watchman again, the news of the city's fall, words of restoration, the valley of bones, Gog, and the vision of a new temple and land (33–48).

outline.title: Shepherd, new heart, dry bones, Gog

One of the twenty-five men at the east gate; he died as Ezekiel prophesied in the vision.

places.name: Ezekiel's tomb (tradition)
places.note: Shown at Kefil near Birs Nimrud (Jewish Encyclopedia, 1903); not in the site's atlas.

scripture.text: The latest date in the book is “the seven and twentieth year, in the first month, in the first day of the month”; the vision of the new temple is dated the twenty-fifth year. Scripture does not tell how Ezekiel's life ended.

tradition.text: Benjamin of Tudela describes “the Synagogue of Ezekiel” by the Euphrates with “the sepulchre of Ezekiel” behind it, said to have been built by King Jeconiah and his people after Evil-merodach released him, with a lamp kept burning day and night over it.
The Jewish Encyclopedia says the traditional burial place “is shown at Kefil near Birs Nimrud”, and that the mausoleum dates “probably from the time of the califs”.

questions.question: From what is “the thirtieth year” of Ezekiel 1:1 counted? (Ezekiel 1:2 makes it the fifth year of Jehoiachin's captivity.)

views.label: From the finding of the law in Josiah's eighteenth year
views.holders: The Targum and Jerome, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876); Ideler

argument.text: Keil reports this reading of “the Chaldee paraphrast and Jerome”, and objects that “no trace … can elsewhere be pointed out of the existence of a chronology dating from these events”.

views.label: From the reign of Nabopolassar of Babylon
views.holders: “Many of the older expositors”, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876)

argument.text: Keil notes that Nabopolassar became king of Babylon in the year this would point to, but that “nothing … is know of any such era”.

views.label: Ezekiel's own age
views.holders: Hengstenberg, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876); E. G. Hirsch and K. H. Cornill in the Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

argument.text: Keil rejects it because the added month and day point “to an era generally recognised”. The Jewish Encyclopedia holds that if the date be understood “to apply to the age of the prophet … this view still has the appearance of probability”.

views.label: Not now known
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1876); S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Keil says the era “is matter of dispute, and can no longer be ascertained with certainty”; Driver says the epoch “is uncertain”.

questions.question: Were the sign-acts done before the people, or seen in vision?

views.label: Seen in vision
views.holders: Kimchi and Maimonides, as reported by John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Gill reports that some think the lying on one side “was not in reality, but in vision, as Kimchi observes; and so Maimonides”, urging that no one could lie so long on one side without a miracle. He judges that “the reasons given on both sides are not despicable.”

views.label: Done in fact
views.holders: The Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897)

argument.text: The Pulpit Commentary writes: “I adopt, without any hesitation, the view that we have here the record of a fact, and not of a vision narrated. The object of the act was to startle men and make them wonder.” Several acts are said to be done “in their sight” and “before their eyes”.

questions.question: What do the dry bones of Ezekiel 37 stand for?

views.label: The nation's return, as the text explains it
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver reads it by verse 11: Israel had “in appearance ceased to be a nation”, and the vision teaches that “God can endow the seemingly dead nation with fresh life, and plant it again in its old land”.

views.label: A pledge of the resurrection of the body
views.holders: Tertullian (early third century)

argument.text: Tertullian grants that the vision may picture a restoration of the Jewish state, but asks “what matters it to me, provided there be also a resurrection of the body”, holding that “the metaphor could not have been formed from bones, if the same thing exactly were not to be realized in them also”.

views.label: The nation's restoration, with its last fulfilment at the general resurrection
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1876)

argument.text: Keil writes that the vision's “ultimate fulfilment … will not take place till the general resurrection”.

views.label: A real raising of dead men in Ezekiel's day
views.holders: Rabbinic traditions, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

argument.text: The Jewish Encyclopedia reports traditions that the bones were men actually raised by Ezekiel, and notes that “as early as the second century, however, some authorities declared this resurrection of the dead was a prophetic vision”.

questions.question: How is the temple vision of Ezekiel 40–48 to be read? (C. F. Keil, 1876, sets out the readings below.)

views.label: A pattern for rebuilding after the return
views.holders: “Many of the Jews” according to Jerome; Grotius, Dathe, Eichhorn, Herder and Böttcher, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876)

argument.text: Keil reports this reading, that Ezekiel describes the temple of Solomon “as a model for the rebuilding of it after the return of the Jews from the captivity”, and objects that it cannot explain the river from the threshold or the separation of the temple from the city.

views.label: A constitution for the restored community, partly ideal
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891); Ewald, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876)

argument.text: Driver calls chapters 40–48 “the constitution of the restored theocracy”, founded on pre-exilic practice, but with “an ideal element in Ezek.'s representations, which in many respects it was found in the event impossible to put into practice”.

views.label: A temple and worship to be literally restored in the future
views.holders: Jewish expectation; among Christians M. Baumgarten, and more guardedly Auberlen, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876)

argument.text: Keil reports that the literal interpretation “remained for a long time peculiar to the Jews”, who expect “the rebuilding of the temple and the renewal of the Levitical worship in the manner described by Ezekiel”, and that some recent Christian writers taught a rebuilt temple in a millennial kingdom. Of Auberlen, Keil says he “has only hinted at this”.

views.label: A figure of the kingdom of God, not to be built
views.holders: Ephraem Syrus, Theodoret and Jerome, as reported by C. F. Keil (1876); Keil himself

argument.text: Keil holds the “symbolico-typical view”, that the vision “can only be interpreted in a typical sense”, and reports that it “gained the upper hand at a very early period in the Christian church”.

questions.question: Did Nebuchadnezzar take Tyre, as Ezekiel 26 foretold? (Ezekiel 29:18 says he had “no wages” for his service against it.)

views.label: He besieged it but did not take it
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver writes that the siege lasted thirteen years according to Josephus “(quoting from Phoenician sources)”, and that Nebuchadnezzar “did not, as Ezek. himself owns (29, 18), succeed in reducing it”. Josephus's Phoenician record says only: “Nabuchodonosor besieged Tyre for thirteen years in the days of Ithobal, their king”.

views.label: Whether he took it is not known; 29:18 speaks only of no spoil
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1876)

argument.text: Keil answers that “the assumption that the city was not taken is a mere conjecture”, and that the siege was in any case a service done for the LORD.

notSaid: Ezekiel does not say how old he was, or from what “the thirtieth year” (Ezek 1:1) is counted.
Ezekiel 4 does not say from when the 390 and 40 years of iniquity are reckoned.
Ezekiel never names Zedekiah, the Pharaoh of chapters 29–32, or the prince of Tyrus.
The text does not itself connect “yet shall he not see it” (Ezek 12:13) with the blinding of Zedekiah in 2 Kings 25:7; the reader is left to compare them.
The New Testament does not name Ezekiel.
Scripture does not say how, when or where Ezekiel died.

prophets.name: Haggai
prophets.title: “Haggai the LORD’s messenger in the LORD’s message” (Haggai 1:13)
prophets.tagline: Four dated words in the second year of Darius: build the house.

claim.text: Haggai names the year, “the second year of Darius the king”, at his first word, at the start of the work and (as “the second year of Darius”) at his third word. His words fall on the first day of the sixth month, the twenty-first day of the seventh, and twice on the twenty-fourth day of the ninth (the last says only “the four and twentieth day of the month”). The work on the house began on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month.

quote.text: In the second year of Darius the king, in the sixth month, in the first day of the month, came the word of the LORD by Haggai the prophet

claim.text: Haggai's first and second words were sent to Zerubbabel and to Joshua the high priest, and his last to Zerubbabel alone, with the promise of the signet.

quote.text: will I take thee, O Zerubbabel, my servant, the son of Shealtiel, saith the LORD, and will make thee as a signet: for I have chosen thee
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?

claim.text: Haggai's book records no call. It opens with the word that came “by Haggai the prophet” to Zerubbabel and Joshua on the first day of the sixth month of Darius's second year: the people said “The time is not come” to build the LORD's house.

how.text: The word of the LORD came “by Haggai the prophet”, and once “unto Haggai”.
He is called “the LORD’s messenger in the LORD’s message”, and the people obeyed his words “as the LORD their God had sent him”.

He put two questions of the law to the priests, whether holy flesh makes food holy and whether one unclean by a dead body makes it unclean, and drew the lesson: “So is this people, and so is this nation before me”.

Ezra says “Haggai the prophet, and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied unto the Jews that were in Judah and Jerusalem”, and that when the building began again “the prophets of God” were “helping them”.
Every word in the book is dated to the day.

Keil (1868) takes this Darius to be Darius Hystaspes (Darius I): Zechariah, he writes, began “in the second year of Darius Hystaspes, only two months later than his contemporary Haggai”. On Parker and Dubberstein's tables (1942), the second year of Darius I began on 3 April 520 BC, and the first day of its sixth month, the day of Haggai's first word, fell on 29 August 520 BC.

message.theme: First the house of the LORD

claim.text: The people dwelt in “cieled houses” while the LORD's house lay waste; they are told to go up to the mountain, bring wood and build.

quotes.text: Go up to the mountain, and bring wood, and build the house; and I will take pleasure in it, and I will be glorified, saith the LORD.

claim.text: They sowed much and brought in little; the LORD called for a drought, smote them with blasting and mildew and hail; from the day the foundation was laid he would bless them.

from this day will I bless you

quotes.text: be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you, saith the LORD of hosts

claim.text: To those who saw the house as nothing beside its first glory, the LORD says he will shake heaven and earth and all nations, fill the house with glory, and give peace in that place.

quotes.text: The glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former, saith the LORD of hosts

quote.text: Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest
If one that is unclean by a dead body touch any of these, shall it be unclean?
I will shake the heavens and the earth

reported.text: Zerubbabel, Joshua, “with all the remnant of the people, obeyed the voice of the LORD their God, and the words of Haggai the prophet”, and on the twenty-fourth day of the sixth month “they came and did work in the house of the LORD of hosts”.

word.text: “Be strong … and work: for I am with you, saith the LORD of hosts”.

reported.text: Ezra: “they prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. And they builded, and finished it”, on the third day of Adar in the sixth year of Darius.

claim.text: Two chapters: four words, each dated to the day in the second year of Darius, all concerned with building the LORD's house, and the people's response between them.

The glory of the latter house
Unclean, and blessed from this day

quotedInNT.note: Quoted: “now he hath promised, saying, Yet once more I shake not the earth only, but also heaven.”

claim.text: Ezra names the two prophets together, prophesying to the Jews and helping the builders.
“Governor of Judah”, to whom three of Haggai's four words were sent; the LORD “stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel”.
“The high priest”, addressed with Zerubbabel in Haggai's first and second words; Ezra calls him “Jeshua the son of Jozadak”.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where the house of the LORD was rebuilt.

scripture.text: Haggai's last dated word is the twenty-fourth day of the ninth month of Darius's second year. Ezra adds that the house was finished in Darius's sixth year through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah. Scripture says nothing more of him.

tradition.text: According to tradition, as the Jewish Encyclopedia reports it, Haggai “was born in Chaldea during the Captivity, and was among those that returned under Zerubbabel”, and is numbered among “the men of the Great Synagogue” (Talmud, Baba Batra 15a).
tradition.who: Jewish tradition, as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia

tradition.text: His name, the Jewish Encyclopedia notes, stands in the Septuagint titles of some psalms, “though not in all manuscripts alike”.

questions.question: What is “the desire of all nations” that “shall come” (Haggai 2:7)?

views.label: A person: the Messiah
views.holders: The Targum and the Vulgate, as reported by the Pulpit Commentary; Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871)

argument.text: The Pulpit Commentary reports that this is “the rendering of the ancient Jewish expositors, the Chaldee Targum, and the Vulgate, which gives, Veniet desideratus cunctis gentibus”, though it notes the difficulty that the verb is plural. Jamieson, Fausset and Brown hold that the Messiah is meant, as the one who satisfies the longings of the nations.

views.label: The precious things of the nations, brought to the house
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868); Ellicott's Commentary; S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Keil reads it as “the valuable possessions of the heathen, or according to Haggai 2:8 their gold and silver”. Ellicott renders “the precious things of all the nations shall come”, calling the Authorised Version's rendering “grammatically impossible with the present text, for the verb ‘come’ is plural”. Driver speaks of the glory coming from “the munificence of the Gentiles”.

notSaid: Scripture gives Haggai no father, tribe or home.
Haggai 2:3 asks who among the people had seen the house “in her first glory”; it does not say whether Haggai had.
Scripture does not say when or where Haggai died.

prophets.name: Zechariah
prophets.title: “Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo the prophet” (Zechariah 1:1)
prophets.tagline: Night visions in the second year of Darius; the fasts in the fourth; two burdens after.

claim.text: Zechariah dates his words by Darius: “in the eighth month, in the second year of Darius”; the visions on “the four and twentieth day of the eleventh month, which is the month Sebat”; and the answer about the fasts “in the fourth year of king Darius … in the fourth day of the ninth month, even in Chisleu”.

quote.text: In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, came the word of the LORD unto Zechariah

claim.text: In the vision of the candlestick came “the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel”: the great mountain would become a plain before him, and his hands, which laid the foundation of the house, would finish it.

quote.text: Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.

call.label: The first word: Turn ye unto me

quote.text: Turn ye unto me, saith the LORD of hosts, and I will turn unto you, saith the LORD of hosts.

claim.text: Zechariah's book records no call. It opens with the word of the eighth month of Darius's second year: not to be like the fathers, who did not hear the former prophets.

how.text: He saw visions “by night”, and asked “the angel that talked with me” what they meant.
He was told to take silver and gold from the returned exiles, make crowns and set them on the head of Joshua the high priest.
He was told to “feed the flock of the slaughter” with two staves called Beauty and Bands, and later to take “the instruments of a foolish shepherd”.
Chapters 9 and 12 open with “The burden of the word of the LORD”.
When Sherezer and Regem-melech asked the priests and prophets whether to keep weeping in the fifth month, the word came to Zechariah.
Ezra names him “Zechariah the son of Iddo” and says the elders “prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah”.

Keil (1868) takes this Darius to be Darius Hystaspes (Darius I): Zechariah, he writes, began “in the second year of Darius Hystaspes, only two months later than his contemporary Haggai”. On Parker and Dubberstein's tables (1942), the second year of Darius I ran from spring 520 BC to spring 519 BC, and his fourth year began in spring 518 BC.

claim.text: The fathers did not hear the former prophets, and the LORD's words “did … take hold of your fathers”; now he calls the people to turn to him.

quotes.text: Be ye not as your fathers, unto whom the former prophets have cried

message.theme: Jealous for Jerusalem; the house shall be built

claim.text: The LORD is jealous for Jerusalem and Zion, has returned with mercies, and will dwell in her midst; old men and old women will again sit in her streets.

quotes.text: I am returned to Jerusalem with mercies: my house shall be built in it, saith the LORD of hosts

message.theme: Not by might, nor by power

claim.text: The work will be done by the LORD's spirit; “who hath despised the day of small things?”

quotes.text: Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts.

message.theme: Judgment and mercy rather than fasts

claim.text: Asked about the fasts, the LORD asks whether they fasted to him at all, and repeats the word of the former prophets: true judgment, mercy, and no oppression of the widow, the fatherless, the stranger or the poor. The fasts will become feasts.

quotes.text: Execute true judgment, and shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother

message.theme: Many nations shall be joined to the LORD

claim.text: Many people and strong nations will come to seek the LORD in Jerusalem.

quotes.text: We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you.

claim.text: The daughter of Zion is told to rejoice, for her King comes “lowly, and riding upon an ass”, and will speak peace to the heathen.

quotes.text: behold, thy King cometh unto thee: he is just, and having salvation; lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass

claim.text: All nations gather against Jerusalem; the LORD's feet stand on the mount of Olives; living waters go out from Jerusalem; the LORD shall be king over all the earth.

quotes.text: And the LORD shall be king over all the earth: in that day shall there be one LORD, and his name one.

quote.text: Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, thou, and thy fellows that sit before thee
Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain

words.to: The people of the land and the priests

quote.text: When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, did ye at all fast unto me, even to me?
Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Zion; shout, O daughter of Jerusalem: behold, thy King cometh unto thee
The burden of the word of the LORD in the land of Hadrach, and Damascus shall be the rest thereof
Woe to the idol shepherd that leaveth the flock!

signs.label: The man among the myrtle trees

claim.text: A man on a red horse among myrtle trees, with red, speckled and white horses behind, reports that all the earth “sitteth still, and is at rest”; the angel of the LORD asks how long the LORD will not have mercy on Jerusalem, and is answered “with good words and comfortable words”.
Four horns are “the horns which have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem”; four carpenters come “to fray them”.
A man goes to measure Jerusalem, but it shall be inhabited “as towns without walls”, and the LORD will be “a wall of fire round about”.

Joshua the high priest stands in filthy garments with Satan at his right hand to resist him; “The LORD rebuke thee, O Satan”; he is clothed with change of raiment and a fair mitre, and told “I will bring forth my servant the BRANCH”.

signs.label: The candlestick and two olive trees

claim.text: A golden candlestick with seven lamps, and two olive trees beside it, which are “the two anointed ones, that stand by the Lord of the whole earth”; with it the word to Zerubbabel.
A roll twenty cubits long and ten broad: “the curse that goeth forth over the face of the whole earth”, entering the house of the thief and of the false swearer.
A woman sitting in an ephah, “This is wickedness”, shut in with a talent of lead and carried by two winged women “to build it an house in the land of Shinar”.
Four chariots with red, black, white, and grisled and bay horses come out from between two mountains of brass: “the four spirits of the heavens”.

Of the silver and gold of Heldai, Tobijah and Jedaiah, come from Babylon, he was to make crowns and set them on Joshua's head: “Behold the man whose name is The BRANCH … he shall build the temple of the LORD”. The crowns were to be a memorial in the temple.

signs.label: The two staves and the thirty pieces

claim.text: Feeding “the flock of slaughter”, he took two staves, Beauty and Bands, and broke Beauty. Asked for his price, they weighed him thirty pieces of silver, and the LORD said, “Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prised at of them.” Then he broke Bands, “the brotherhood between Judah and Israel”.
He was told to take “the instruments of a foolish shepherd”, for the LORD would raise up a shepherd who would not care for the flock.

word.text: “The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also finish it”.

reported.text: Ezra: “they prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. And they builded, and finished it”, in the sixth year of Darius. Ezra does not name Zerubbabel at the finishing.

word.text: “Behold, thy King cometh unto thee … lowly, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt the foal of an ass.”

reported.text: Matthew: “All this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet”, when Jesus rode into Jerusalem; John adds that the disciples understood it only after Jesus was glorified.

word.text: “So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver … And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD.”

reported.text: Matthew, of the field bought with Judas's silver: “Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by Jeremy the prophet, saying, And they took the thirty pieces of silver”. Matthew names Jeremy (Jeremiah), not Zechariah.

word.text: “They shall look upon me whom they have pierced, and they shall mourn for him”.

reported.text: John, at the cross: “these things were done, that the scripture should be fulfilled … And again another scripture saith, They shall look on him whom they pierced.”

word.text: “Smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered”.

reported.text: Jesus applied it to the night of his arrest: “All ye shall be offended because of me this night: for it is written, I will smite the shepherd”. At the arrest Matthew writes: “But all this was done, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled. Then all the disciples forsook him, and fled.”

claim.text: Fourteen chapters: a call to return (1:1–6), eight night visions with the crowning of Joshua (1:7–6:15), the answer about the fasts in Darius's fourth year (7–8), and two undated “burdens” (9–11 and 12–14).

Quoted: “as it is written, Fear not, daughter of Sion”.

scripture.text: Zechariah's last dated word is in the fourth year of Darius; Ezra says the house was finished in the sixth year through the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah. Scripture says nothing of his death.

tradition.text: G. L. Robinson writes in the ISBE that “nothing is known of his end. The Targum says he died a martyr.”
tradition.who: The Targum, as reported in the ISBE

questions.question: Son of Berechiah, or son of Iddo, and was he the priest of Nehemiah 12:16? (Zechariah 1:1 has “the son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo”; Ezra 5:1 and 6:14 have “the son of Iddo”; Nehemiah 12:4 names Iddo among the priests who came up with Zerubbabel, and 12:16 has “Of Iddo's, Zechariah” among the heads of priestly houses in the days of Joiakim.)

views.label: Grandson of Iddo, a priest who succeeded him as head of the house
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868); G. L. Robinson in ISBE (1915), conditionally

argument.text: Keil holds that Zechariah “followed his grandfather in that office under the high priest Jehoiakim”, and that “his father died young”, which he thinks may explain why Ezra calls him “the son (grandson) of Iddo”. Robinson writes that the same Iddo “seems to be mentioned” in Nehemiah 12:4, and “if so, Zechariah was a priest as well as a prophet”.

questions.question: Who wrote Zechariah 9–14, and when? (Views in the order they arose.)

views.label: Zechariah himself, after the exile
views.holders: Tradition, as G. L. Robinson in ISBE (1915) holds; he lists among those defending the book's unity C. H. H. Wright (1879) and E. B. Pusey (1877)

argument.text: Robinson concludes that “tradition points to a saner and securer conclusion, that these oracles were written by Zechariah himself”, citing what the two parts share in thought and in diction.

views.label: Jeremiah
views.holders: Joseph Mede, as reported by John Gill (1746–1748)

argument.text: Gill reports that Mede “laboured, by various arguments” to show “that the four last chapters of Zechariah were written by Jeremy”, which would explain why Matthew 27:9 quotes them under Jeremiah's name.

views.label: Before the exile: 9–11 in the eighth century, 12–14 before Jerusalem's fall
views.holders: Abp Newcome, Ewald, Bleek, Hitzig and others, as listed by S. R. Driver (1891)

argument.text: Driver sets out their grounds: the kingdom of the ten tribes seems still to exist (9:10; 11:14), Assyria and Egypt are named together, teraphim are mentioned, and “the mourning of Hadadrimmon” is taken of Josiah's death.

views.label: The Greek period
views.holders: B. Stade, as reported by S. R. Driver (1891); G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Smith writes that Zechariah 9–14 “has been rightly assigned by Stade to the early years of the Greek Period”; Driver notes that the way the Greeks are named in 9:13 is the chief obstacle to an early date.

views.label: Mixed: an eighth-century prophecy (9–11) recast after the exile; 12–14 after the exile
views.holders: S. R. Driver (1891), with Cheyne and Kuenen

argument.text: Driver concludes, “with Prof. Cheyne and Kuenen”, that chapters 9–11 date from the 8th century but were “modified in details, and accommodated to a later situation”, and that 12–14 are post-exilic, adding that “probably no entirely satisfactory explanation of it is now attainable”.

questions.question: Why does Matthew 27:9 quote Zechariah 11:12–13 as “spoken by Jeremy the prophet”?

views.label: Some copies read only “by the prophet”
views.holders: Reported, and not accepted, by Augustine (about 400)

argument.text: Augustine notes that the name “is not contained in all the codices of the Gospels”, but is not satisfied with this answer, since “a majority of codices contain the name of Jeremiah”.

views.label: Matthew's memory, left to stand by the Spirit, to show the prophets speak as one
views.holders: Augustine (about 400)

argument.text: Augustine suggests that “the word Jeremiah occurred to his mind … instead of Zechariah”, and that it was left so that we might accept the prophets' books “as if they formed but a single book written by one author”.

views.label: Matthew joins Jeremiah's field to Zechariah's silver
views.holders: Augustine (about 400)

argument.text: Augustine points out that Jeremiah bought a field, which Zechariah does not mention, while Zechariah has the thirty pieces of silver, so that the evangelist interprets the two together.

views.label: Matthew quoted from memory, recalling Jeremiah's chapters on the potter
views.holders: Ellicott's Commentary

argument.text: Ellicott suggests that “the writer quoted from memory”, recalling “the two conspicuous chapters (18 and 19) in which Jeremiah had spoken of the potter”.

views.label: Jeremiah stood first in the book of the prophets
views.holders: John Lightfoot, as quoted by Jamieson, Fausset and Brown (1871); John Gill (1746–1748)

argument.text: Lightfoot, as quoted, says Matthew “only cites the words of the volume of the prophets under his name who stood first in the volume”. Gill calls this the answer that “seems best to solve this difficulty”.

questions.question: Is the “Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23:35) this Zechariah? (Luke 11:51 says only “Zacharias”.)

views.label: Zechariah son of Jehoiada, with “son of Barachias” a slip
views.holders: Ellicott's Commentary; A. B. Bruce (1897)

argument.text: Ellicott points to the martyrdom of Zechariah son of Jehoiada in 2 Chronicles 24:20–22 and suggests that “son of Barachias” “may be accounted for as the mistake of a transcriber”; he notes that the prophet is “the only ‘Zechariah the son of Barachias’ in the Old Testament”, but that “of his death we know nothing”. Bruce calls the phrase a designation of the minor prophet “applied here to the other Zechariah, by inadvertence either of the evangelist or of an early copyist”. No source used for this page holds that the prophet himself is meant.

notSaid: Zechariah's book does not call him a priest; Nehemiah 12:16 names a Zechariah at the head of Iddo's priestly house.
The book gives no date for chapters 9–14.
Scripture does not say how or when Zechariah died.

prophets.name: Shemaiah son of Delaiah
otherNames: Shemaiah the son of Delaiah the son of Mehetabeel
prophets.title: Hired by Tobiah and Sanballat: “God had not sent him” (Nehemiah 6:12)
prophets.tagline: Urged Nehemiah to hide in the temple; Nehemiah saw that he had been hired.

claim.text: Nehemiah came to Shemaiah's house; Shemaiah urged him to shut himself in the temple because men would come to slay him by night. Nehemiah refused, perceiving “that God had not sent him”.

quote.text: Should such a man as I flee? and who is there, that, being as I am, would go into the temple to save his life? I will not go in.

claim.text: Nehemiah was governor of Judah “from the twentieth year even unto the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes the king”. The plots of chapter 6 came when the wall was built but the doors not yet set up. Scripture does not show this prophet before the king.

how.text: Nehemiah says Shemaiah “pronounced this prophecy against me: for Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him”, so that Nehemiah would be afraid and sin, and his enemies have “matter for an evil report”.
When Nehemiah came to his house, Shemaiah “was shut up”.

claim.text: His one recorded word: meet in the house of God, shut the doors of the temple, for they will come by night to slay thee.

quotes.text: Let us meet together in the house of God, within the temple, and let us shut the doors of the temple: for they will come to slay thee

quote.text: yea, in the night will they come to slay thee

claim.text: His father.
His grandfather.
With Sanballat, “had hired him”.
With Tobiah, hired him “that I should be afraid, and do so, and sin”.
The governor he tried to frighten; Nehemiah asks God to “think thou upon” Tobiah, Sanballat, Noadiah and the rest of the prophets.
“The prophetess Noadiah”, named in the same prayer among those that would have put Nehemiah in fear.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: The house of God, where Shemaiah urged Nehemiah to hide.

scripture.text: Scripture says no more of Shemaiah after Nehemiah 6.

questions.question: What does it mean that Shemaiah “was shut up” (Nehemiah 6:10)?

views.label: Ceremonially unclean
views.holders: Ewald, as reported by C. F. Keil (1873)

argument.text: Keil reports this reading and rejects it.

views.label: Held by a higher power, so that Nehemiah had to come to him
views.holders: Bertheau, as reported by C. F. Keil (1873)

argument.text: Keil reports Bertheau's reading, “overpowered by the hand of Jahve”, and answers that Shemaiah's own proposal to go to the temple shows he was not prevented from leaving home.

views.label: Shut in his house, feigning that his own life was in danger, perhaps as a sign
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1873)

argument.text: Keil holds that “he had shut himself in his house, to intimate to Nehemiah that also he felt his life in danger”; whether this was feigned or a symbolic act, “either view is possible”.

notSaid: Nehemiah does not say how he perceived that God had not sent Shemaiah.
Scripture does not say what became of Shemaiah.

prophets.name: Noadiah
prophets.title: “The prophetess Noadiah” (Nehemiah 6:14)
prophets.tagline: Named once, among the prophets who would have put Nehemiah in fear.

claim.text: Nehemiah names her in a prayer, after telling how Shemaiah was hired against him.

quote.text: My God, think thou upon Tobiah and Sanballat according to these their works, and on the prophetess Noadiah, and the rest of the prophets, that would have put me in fear.

claim.text: Nehemiah was governor of Judah “from the twentieth year even unto the two and thirtieth year of Artaxerxes the king”. The plots of chapter 6 came when the wall was built but the doors not yet set up. Scripture does not show this prophetess before the king.

how.text: She is called “the prophetess”. Nehemiah records nothing she said; he names her with “the rest of the prophets, that would have put me in fear”.

claim.text: Named first in the same prayer.
Named with Tobiah in the same prayer.
The prophet Tobiah and Sanballat had hired, whose story comes just before her name.
The governor she and the other prophets “would have put … in fear”.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where the wall was finished in fifty-two days.

scripture.text: Scripture names her once and says no more of her.

questions.question: Who was Noadiah, and was she hired like Shemaiah? (Nehemiah 6:14 says only that she was among those “that would have put me in fear”.)

views.label: A false prophetess, in the same scheme as Shemaiah
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–1685); John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Poole calls her “one that falsely pretended to the Spirit of prophecy, to deceive and destroy Nehemiah”. Gill holds that she was “a false prophetess, and was hired, and in the same scheme with Shemaiah”.

views.label: Possibly bribed, but this is uncertain
views.holders: Ewald, as reported by the Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897)

argument.text: The Pulpit Commentary reports that she “has been supposed to have succumbed to a bribe, like Shemaiah (Ewald); but this is wholly uncertain. We only know that, together with certain soi-disant prophets, she endeavoured to ‘put Nehemiah in fear.’”

views.label: The same person as Shemaiah
views.holders: Aben Ezra, as reported by John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Gill reports that Aben Ezra took Noadiah to be Shemaiah, because Shemaiah said “let us meet”; Gill answers that “no doubt it is the name of a woman”.

views.label: A man: “Noadiah the prophet”
views.holders: The Septuagint, as reported by H. E. Ryle (1893)

argument.text: Ryle notes that “the LXX. and possibly the Vulgate regarded ‘Noadiah’ as masc.” The King James text, following the Hebrew, says “the prophetess”.

notSaid: Scripture does not say what Noadiah prophesied, whether she was paid, or that God had not sent her; it says only that she was among those that “would have put me in fear”.
Scripture gives her no father, husband or home.

prophets.name: Malachi
prophets.title: “The burden of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi” (Malachi 1:1)
prophets.tagline: A dispute with priests and people, ending with Moses and Elijah.

how.text: The book is headed “The burden of the word of the LORD to Israel by Malachi”, and says nothing else of him.
The book is set out as a dispute: the LORD speaks, the people's objection is quoted (“Yet ye say, Wherein…?”), and the LORD answers.
G. A. Smith (1898) notes that “Malachi” could mean “My Angel or Messenger”, the same word as in 3:1, “Behold, I send My messenger”.
The book speaks to a people under a governor (“offer it now unto thy governor”) and with a temple and altar in use.

claim.text: To the question “Wherein hast thou loved us?” the LORD answers with Jacob and Esau, and the laying waste of Edom's mountains.

quotes.text: I have loved you, saith the LORD. Yet ye say, Wherein hast thou loved us?

claim.text: The priests despise the LORD's name by offering the blind, the lame and the sick; the covenant of Levi was life and peace, but they have caused many to stumble; yet in every place his name shall be great among the heathen.

quotes.text: if then I be a father, where is mine honour? and if I be a master, where is my fear?

claim.text: Judah has married “the daughter of a strange god”, and men have dealt treacherously with “the wife of thy youth”.

quotes.text: For the LORD, the God of Israel, saith that he hateth putting away

message.theme: The messenger and the Lord's coming

claim.text: To those who ask “Where is the God of judgment?”: the LORD will send his messenger, and the Lord will come suddenly to his temple as a refiner, to purify the sons of Levi and judge the wicked.

quotes.text: Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple

claim.text: They have robbed God “in tithes and offerings”; if they bring the tithes into the storehouse he will open the windows of heaven.

quotes.text: Return unto me, and I will return unto you, saith the LORD of hosts.

message.theme: A book of remembrance and the day that cometh

claim.text: Those who feared the LORD spoke often one to another, and a book of remembrance was written; the day comes that shall burn as an oven, but to those who fear his name the Sun of righteousness shall arise.

quotes.text: But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings

claim.text: The book ends: remember the law of Moses; the LORD will send Elijah the prophet before the great and dreadful day.

quotes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD

Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.

word.text: “Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me”.

reported.text: Jesus says of John the Baptist: “this is he, of whom it is written, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face”. Mark opens his Gospel with the same words, “As it is written in the prophets”.

word.text: “Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the LORD”, to turn the heart of the fathers to the children.

reported.text: The angel says John “shall go before him in the spirit and power of Elias, to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children”. Jesus says “if ye will receive it, this is Elias, which was for to come”, and “Elias is come already”, and the disciples understood “that he spake unto them of John the Baptist”. Asked “Art thou Elias?”, John himself answered, “I am not.”

claim.text: Four chapters in the King James Version, set out as a dispute between the LORD and his people and priests, ending with the call to remember the law of Moses and the promise of Elijah.

scripture.text: Scripture says nothing of Malachi beyond the heading of his book.

tradition.text: A tradition preserved in the Lives of the Prophets ascribed to Epiphanius, as the Jewish Encyclopedia reports it, makes Malachi “of the tribe of Zebulun”, born after the Captivity, and says “he died young, and was buried in his own country with his fathers”.
tradition.who: pseudo-Epiphanius, Lives of the Prophets, as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia

tradition.text: A rabbinic saying runs: “After the death of the last three prophets, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, the Holy Spirit departed from Israel”.
tradition.who: Tosefta, Sotah 13.2, as quoted in the Jewish Encyclopedia

questions.question: Is “Malachi” a name, or a title? (Views roughly in the order they arose.)

views.label: A title, “his messenger”, not a name
views.holders: The Septuagint, as reported by S. R. Driver (1891) and G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Driver and Smith note that the Greek translators read 1:1 as “by the hand of his messenger”.

views.label: Ezra the scribe
views.holders: The Targum of Jonathan; Joshua ben Karha in the Talmud (Megillah 15a); Jerome, who reports it

argument.text: The Targum adds to “by the hand of Malachi” the words “whose name is called Ezra the scribe”. The Jewish Encyclopedia reports that Jerome knew the belief that Malachi was Ezra, and that the Talmud also records an identification with Mordecai. Driver answers that had Ezra been the author, “it is difficult to think that his authorship would have been thus concealed”.

views.label: An official name or a title drawn from 3:1, for an anonymous book
views.holders: Hengstenberg and Vitringa, as reported by C. F. Keil (1868); Ewald, Kuenen, Reuss and Stade, as listed by S. R. Driver (1891); G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Smith holds that “Malachi” is “an anonymous work”, and that the name “was a purely artificial one borrowed from chap. iii. 1, Behold, I send My messenger”, the title being added by the editor of the Twelve, like the headings of Zechariah 9:1 and 12:1.

views.label: The prophet's own name
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868)

argument.text: Keil answers that the arguments for an official name “are not conclusive”: other prophets' headings also give only a name, and names of this form are common.

questions.question: When did Malachi speak? (The book gives no date; it names a governor and a working temple, and the wrongs it rebukes are those Nehemiah fought.)

views.label: Before Ezra came to Jerusalem
views.holders: Herzfeld, Bleek, Reuss and Stade, as listed by S. R. Driver (1891); G. A. Smith (1898)

argument.text: Smith calls the book “an anonymous work from the eve of Ezra's reforms”.

views.label: In Nehemiah's time, during or near his absence at the Persian court
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1868); S. R. Driver (1891), with Schrader, Köhler, Orelli and Kuenen

argument.text: Keil places it after Nehemiah's return to the king in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes. Driver judges “the period of Nehemiah's absence at the Persian Court is the most probable”, since the governor of 1:8 seems not to be Nehemiah himself.

notSaid: Scripture gives Malachi no father, home, tribe or date.
Malachi names no king; he speaks only of “thy governor” (Mal 1:8).
Scripture does not say how or when Malachi died.
